# Mathematical toolbox and notation {#sec-toolbox}

## Vectors, operators, and traces

A finite-dimensional Hilbert space is a complex vector space with inner
product $\langle u|v\rangle$, conjugate-linear in $u$ and linear in $v$.
An orthonormal basis obeys $\langle i|j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$ and
$\sum_i|i\rangle\langle i|=I$. Components are
$v_i=\langle i|v\rangle$, and the adjoint satisfies
$\langle u|Av\rangle=\langle A^\dagger u|v\rangle$.

A Hermitian matrix obeys $A^\dagger=A$ and has an orthonormal eigenbasis with
real eigenvalues. A positive matrix has nonnegative eigenvalues.
A unitary obeys $U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I$.
The group $U(d)$ is the set of all $d$-dimensional unitaries; $SU(d)$ restricts
their determinants to one. Global phases disappear from state projectors,
but conventions about the group still matter for operator moments.

The trace $\operatorname{Tr}A=\sum_i\langle i|A|i\rangle$ is independent of
orthonormal basis. Cyclicity,
$\operatorname{Tr}(AB)=\operatorname{Tr}(BA)$, follows by writing
$\sum_{ij}A_{ij}B_{ji}$. Factors can be rotated cyclically, but cannot
generally be reordered arbitrarily.
The commutator is $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and anticommutator is $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$.

For tensor products,
$(A\otimes B)(C\otimes D)=AC\otimes BD$ and
$\operatorname{Tr}(A\otimes B)=\operatorname{Tr}A\operatorname{Tr}B$.
These identities explain why a product observable on $k$ copies measures
a product of single-copy expectation values.

## Singular values and best low-rank approximations

Any rectangular complex matrix can be written $A=USV^\dagger$, with
orthonormal columns in $U,V$ and nonnegative singular values $s_i$ in $S$.
They are square roots of eigenvalues of $A^\dagger A$.
This is singular-value decomposition, or SVD. Reshaping a bipartite state's
coefficients into a matrix turns its SVD into the Schmidt decomposition.

To approximate $A$ by a matrix of rank at most $\chi$ in Hilbert–Schmidt norm,
keep its $\chi$ largest singular values. The squared error is
$\sum_{i>\chi}s_i^2$. One way to see optimality is to project onto the
candidate approximation's column space. The missed squared norm is minimized
by the subspace carrying the largest eigenvalues of $AA^\dagger$.
No rank-$\chi$ matrix can recover the component perpendicular to that space.

Successive SVDs along a chain yield a matrix product representation.
Truncating many bonds needs an accumulated error analysis; the error from
one cut cannot simply be asserted to control the whole contracted process.

## Norms, dimensions, and contraction

The operator, Hilbert–Schmidt, and trace norms are
$\|A\|_\infty=\max_i s_i$,
$\|A\|_2=(\sum_is_i^2)^{1/2}$, and $\|A\|_1=\sum_is_i$.
For rank at most $r$,

$$
\|A\|_2\leq\|A\|_1\leq\sqrt r\,\|A\|_2.
$$ {#eq-tb-norms}

The second inequality is Cauchy–Schwarz on the singular values.
For Hermitian $X$ with zero trace, write its positive and negative spectral
parts as $X=X_+-X_-$. They have equal trace, and

$$
\frac12\|X\|_1=\max_{0\leq E\leq I}\operatorname{Tr}(EX)
=\max_{0\leq E\leq I}|\operatorname{Tr}(EX)|.
$$ {#eq-tb-variation}

The maximizing effect is the positive spectral projector, or the negative
one for the opposite sign. This formula directly proves contraction under a
CPTP map $\Phi$. Its adjoint is defined by
$\operatorname{Tr}[E\Phi(X)]=\operatorname{Tr}[\Phi^\dagger(E)X]$.
Positivity and trace preservation imply
$0\leq\Phi^\dagger(E)\leq I$, since $\Phi^\dagger(I)=I$.
Maximizing over this subset of effects cannot exceed the maximum over all
effects. Therefore $D(\Phi(\rho),\Phi(\sigma))\leq D(\rho,\sigma)$.
Partial trace is a special case.

Trace distance is sensitive to all measurements. A norm on one selected
family of observables can be weaker and more appropriate operationally,
but must be specified explicitly.

## Gaussian integrals, Wick contractions, and Haar moments

For a standard complex Gaussian $g$ with density $e^{-|g|^2}/\pi$,

$$
\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{d^2g}{\pi}e^{-|g|^2+tg+sg^*}=e^{ts}.
$$

The identity follows by completing squares in the two real components,
or expanding the angular and radial integrals. Differentiating at
$t=s=0$ shows that
$\mathbb E[g^m(g^*)^n]=\delta_{mn}m!$.
For independent components the generating function is
$\exp(\sum_at_as_a)$, so

$$
\mathbb E[g_{i_1}\cdots g_{i_k}g^*_{j_1}\cdots g^*_{j_k}]
=\sum_{\pi\in S_k}\prod_{\ell=1}^k\delta_{i_\ell,j_{\pi(\ell)}}.
$$ {#eq-tb-wick}

Every pairing of an unstarred component with a starred one contributes.
This is the complex Gaussian Wick identity.

Write $g=r\psi$, with $\psi$ a unit vector. Isotropy makes the direction
Haar-distributed and independent of $r$. Since $r^2$ is the sum of $d$
independent exponential variables, its density is
$s^{d-1}e^{-s}/\Gamma(d)$. The gamma integral gives
$\mathbb E[r^{2k}]=\Gamma(d+k)/\Gamma(d)=d(d+1)\cdots(d+k-1)$.
Dividing @eq-tb-wick by that radial moment gives

$$
\mathbb E[\psi_{i_1}\cdots\psi_{i_k}
\psi^*_{j_1}\cdots\psi^*_{j_k}]
=\frac{\sum_{\pi\in S_k}\prod_\ell\delta_{i_\ell,j_{\pi(\ell)}}}
{d(d+1)\cdots(d+k-1)}.
$$ {#eq-tb-haar-components}

The numerator is the matrix element of $\sum_\pi U_\pi$.
Using $P_{\mathrm{sym}}=\sum_\pi U_\pi/k!$ recovers the Haar moment formula
without assuming prior knowledge of representation theory.

The gamma function is
$\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty s^{a-1}e^{-s}ds$ for $a>0$.
Integration by parts gives $\Gamma(a+1)=a\Gamma(a)$, so
$\Gamma(n+1)=n!$. The beta integral,
$\int_0^1x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}dx=\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b)$,
follows by setting $s=u+v$, $x=u/(u+v)$ in the product of two gamma integrals.

## Why all moments identify a pure-state distribution

Pure-state projectors form a compact subset of the finite-dimensional
space of Hermitian matrices. The entries of $M_k$ are averages of
degree-$k$ polynomials in projector entries. Knowing every $M_k$ therefore
gives the average of every polynomial in those entries.
Polynomials distinguish distinct projectors, include constants, and are
closed under multiplication and conjugation. On this compact space they
approximate continuous functions arbitrarily well (the polynomial
approximation theorem in its Stone–Weierstrass form).
Two probability measures with equal averages of every continuous function
are the same measure.

This explains why all-order moment agreement is such a strong claim.
Agreement through one finite $k$ only determines a finite family of polynomial
statistics. Finite experimental precision weakens the conclusion further.

## Noncommuting limits

A schematic diagnostic $\Delta_k(T,L)$ depends on moment order, observation
time, and system size. None of the following is automatically equivalent:

$$
\lim_{T\to\infty}\Delta_k(T,L)=0
\text{ for each fixed }k,L,\qquad
\lim_{L\to\infty}\Delta_k(T,L)=0
\text{ for each fixed }k,T.
$$

Nor does convergence for every fixed $k$ imply a rate uniform in $k$.
If the required time grows rapidly with $k$ or $L$, exchanging limits can
change the result. The finite-rank design obstruction supplies an immediate
example: a fixed finite number of sampled states cannot reproduce arbitrary
orders even when several low moments are accurate.

Use the same caution with substitution depth $n$ and physical word length
$T_n$. If $T_n=2^n$, a plateau lasting several units of $n$ corresponds to
an exponentially increasing physical time. Uniform averaging over $n$ is
not uniform averaging over the trajectory's microscopic steps.

## A compact glossary

| Term | Meaning in this book |
|---|---|
| Bath / environment | Degrees of freedom outside the retained subsystem |
| Born weight | Probability of a specified measurement outcome |
| Conditional state | State normalized after retaining an outcome |
| Projected ensemble | Bath-outcome-weighted collection of conditional states |
| Temporal ensemble | States sampled along one evolution with a stated clock |
| Moment operator | Average of identical-copy projectors, one label shared across copies |
| Haar ensemble | Unitary-invariant complex pure-state distribution |
| State design | Ensemble matching Haar through a specified moment order |
| Frame potential | Average powered overlap, equivalently purity of a moment |
| Scrooge ensemble | Adjusted deformation of Haar minimizing accessible information at a fixed mean |
| Generalized Scrooge ensemble | Mixture accounting for additional classical constraint information |
| Accessible information | Maximum label information obtainable by measuring the output |
| Coherence | Superposition resource relative to a specified basis |
| Magic | Resource beyond stabilizer states and Clifford operations |
| Fragmentation | Decomposition into dynamically disconnected subspaces |
| Scar | Atypical nonthermal eigenstate or associated special dynamics in an otherwise thermal setting |
| Kraus operator | One conditional operator in a dilation/instrument |
| Channel | Linear completely positive trace-preserving map |
| Instrument | Outcome-resolved completely positive maps summing to a channel |
| Process tensor | Rule assigning outcomes to a sequence of interventions |
| Causal break | Measurement and repreparation that removes system-carried history |
| Temporal entanglement | Entanglement across a specified cut in a temporal tensor representation |
| Prethermal regime | Long intermediate regime controlled by an approximate effective generator |
| Floquet drive | Strictly periodic time dependence |
| Morphic drive | Sequence generated by recursively substituting symbols |

The glossary is a reminder, not a substitute for the definitions and
assumptions in the chapters.
